stem.text: The concentration C of a medication in a patient's blood, in milligrams per liter, during an infusion that settles at 70 milligrams per liter moves toward the settling concentration at a rate proportional to the difference between the settling concentration and C. At time \( t = 0 \) minutes, \( C = 15 \). Using k for the positive constant of proportionality, write a differential equation for C as a function of t and state the initial condition.

worked_solution.text: The dependent variable is C and the independent variable is t in minutes, so the rate is \( \frac{dC}{dt} \).

Proportional to the difference means a constant multiple of it. With k positive, \( k(70 - C) \) is positive when C is below 70 and negative when it is above, so C moves up toward 70 from its starting value.
The equation is \( \frac{dC}{dt} = k\left(70 - C\right) \), and the initial condition, stated separately, is \( C(0) = 15 \).

options.label: \( \frac{dC}{dt} = k\left(70 - 15\right) \), with \( C(0) = 15 \)
options.derivation: the initial value 15 substituted for C inside the equation, so the rate becomes a constant

options.label: \( \frac{dC}{dt} = k\left(C - 70\right) \), with \( C(0) = 15 \)
options.derivation: the difference written as C minus the level, which with k positive drives C away from 70

options.label: \( \frac{dC}{dt} = 70 - C \), with \( C(0) = 15 \)
options.derivation: proportional read as equal, so the constant k never appears
